issues.desc: Per-page fan-out: for each Client row -> _build_client_item -> per Project -> _build_project_item does 3 awaits (competitors, platforms, question_count). For page_size=20 with ~5 projects/client = ~300 sequential awaits.
High-frequency admin listing endpoint with no server-side cache; recomputes the same competitor/platform/count aggregates on every request.
page_size=0 falls back to building ALL clients' item graph in a single async coroutine; with hundreds of clients this is unbounded work and locks the request handler.

17 sequential DELETE statements (analysis/crawler/platform schemas) all inside one transaction. With large crawl_answers / reference data this can hold row locks for minutes and exhaust connection pool.
Each delete runs as a separate await db.execute; could be merged into a single CTE-based DELETE for ~10x throughput.
No try/except: if any DELETE in the middle fails the whole transaction aborts and the user is left with a partially-cleaned client. Operator must manually reconcile.
_rebuild_competitors loops await db.delete() once per old competitor (not bulk DELETE WHERE). Update of an 8-competitor project = 8 round-trips inside the same transaction.
For each project to be deleted, again loops await db.delete() per competitor then await db.delete(brand) - serializable sequence.
Mixes fetch + per-row mutate + per-row fetch + bulk insert; on large clients the request handler is held for the full sequence.

_build_project_item issues 3 awaited queries per call (competitors, platforms via QuestionPool, count). Called for every project inside the per-client loop in get_client_list. The classic admin-list N+1.
Project aggregates (question_count, platform union) change slowly. Suitable for a short-TTL cache (e.g. 60s) keyed by project_id+date.

Per-feature loop: SELECT ... WHERE client_id+feature_key, then UPDATE or INSERT. For a 10-feature update = 10 round-trips; should use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (PostgreSQL upsert) in one query.
Feature list is essentially static per client; no read-side cache on get_client_features either.
For each active server, issues a separate SELECT against CrawlerSchedule by server_id (UUID). 20 servers = 20 round-trips. Should be one IN(...) query.
Polled by admin UI frequently; aggregates task_daily_stats / crawl_answers by platform on every call with no cache.

Builds SQL with f-string (where_clause, pagination_clause). All values are bound parameters so no injection, but the dynamic SQL is harder to audit and plan-cache friendly. Prefer sqlalchemy.sql.composed.
page_size=0 returns the entire crawl_answers aggregation; with months of data this can be 100k+ rows serialized into one response.
Dynamic placeholders for project_ids; parameters are bound so safe, but the SQL is re-built per request preventing plan reuse. Use array binding (project_id = ANY(:project_ids)).
page_size=0 returns all matching error rows; with crawl_error_logs growing unbounded this is a memory bomb.
For each server, fires SELECT CrawlerSchedule WHERE server_id=uuid. 10 servers = 10 round-trips. One IN(...) join would do.
Server list is essentially static; no Redis/in-memory cache. CrawlerServers.last_heartbeat is the only hot field.
Loads ALL CrawlerServers into memory just to resolve a single schedule's server name. For 100+ servers this is 100x more data than needed and bypasses the index on server_id.
Server-name lookup is hot; a small LRU keyed by UUID would save the full table scan.
Loads all servers AND all schedules, then resolves server_name with a Python dict. Acceptable for full list, but pair with a single JOIN for the data path.

Top-of-dashboard endpoint, polled every few seconds by admin UI. Issues 6 separate count queries + 2 day-stats queries (task_daily_stats and platform fallback) on every call. No Redis cache despite the data changing at most once per minute.
All queries are awaited sequentially (6 await db.execute calls in series). Could be batched with a single CTE returning all counters in one round-trip.

_get_platform_status loops and for each platform row issues another SELECT MAX(TaskQueue.completed_at) - per-platform round-trip. Should aggregate all in one query with a single MAX(completed_at) grouped by platform.
Today's crawl totals (task_daily_stats) are append-only per day - perfect cache candidate (TTL = until next minute). Yet it is recomputed on every dashboard refresh.
text("...") with :today bound param - safe but raw SQL; better expressed with select() on the ORM model for plan-cache reuse.

After aggregating today's stats per platform, the function loops and for each platform issues a separate SELECT MAX(TaskQueue.completed_at) WHERE target_platform=?. For 5 platforms = 5 extra round-trips. Single GROUP BY query is enough.
Status (healthy/warning/error) is derived from today's counters and last_crawl. Stable for seconds-to-minutes. No cache; high-frequency endpoint.
Same today-stats aggregation as _get_today_crawl_summary, no cache. Two separate endpoints recompute overlapping data.
Uses f-string INTERVAL '{interval}' - interval is from a static map so safe, but raw SQL prevents easy migration and breaks plan caching per distinct value.
Bare `except Exception as e: logger.warning(...); rows = []` swallows DB errors silently. Operator gets an empty dashboard with no alert - could mask outages.
Computes a 4-table JOIN (clients, projects, brand_mention_daily, brand_answer_metrics) on every refresh. Time-range sliding window means cache TTL = a few minutes is safe.
After the big trend query, runs a separate SELECT Projects query for client_projects map. Could be folded into the main CTE.

Four separate `except Exception` blocks silently downgrade to defaults. The dashboard then shows 'pending' / 0% success and operators think the pipeline is broken when in fact the query itself errored.
Endpoint runs 7+ queries (3 status groups + 4 trend CTEs). Polled by admin UI; data freshness is sub-minute. No cache.
The trend 7d CTE is fine, but it is preceded by 6 separate earlier queries that could be a single CTE returning all status counters.

The prev_g query has a correlated subquery `(SELECT MAX(gs2.batch_date) - INTERVAL '1 day' FROM gpower_scores gs2 WHERE gs2.project_id = gs.project_id ...)` - PostgreSQL may not be able to decorrelate this, leading to nested-loop execution per project row.
Heavy CTE + subquery pipeline runs on every dashboard refresh with no cache. Time-range stable; ideal Redis candidate (TTL 60-300s).
Two `except Exception as e: logger.warning(...)` blocks silently fall back. On DB hiccup operators get a half-populated KPI page with no signal.
Deletes old records via `for record in old_result.scalars().all(): await db.delete(record)` - one await per row. Should be a single DELETE WHERE user_id=... with bulk_insert_mappings for inserts.
Per-item db.add + await db.flush() pattern is fine for small N, but the surrounding delete-N is the bottleneck.

For each key row in the paged result, calls `await list_api_key_resources(db, key_row.id)` - per-row query. With page_size=20 and 5 resources/key = 100 extra round-trips per page. Should be a single JOIN with GROUP BY/array_agg.
API key listings are admin-only but still polled; resource permissions rarely change. Short-TTL cache (60s) is safe.
After permission replacement, calls `list_api_key_resources` again to build the response - same per-row join could be avoided by returning the keys that were just written.
Loops DEFAULT_OPEN_API_RESOURCE_KEYS and per-key does `existing.get(resource_key)` then UPDATE or INSERT. Should be INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE in one statement for the full set.
Each row is set with `row.is_allowed = ...; row.granted_by = ...` - 3 round-trips per resource. ORM unit-of-work would help here.
Per project: 3 awaited queries (client_name, competitors, platforms, question_count) inside _build_project_item. page_size=20 with average 1 project = 80+ awaits per page.
Project aggregates change slowly; no cache on the listing endpoint. A 60s Redis cache would cut DB load dramatically.
page_size=0 returns the full project set with all of its aggregates - unbounded.
`for comp in comps_result.scalars().all(): await db.delete(comp)` - per-competitor delete, not a bulk DELETE WHERE project_id=...|project_id IS NULL.
Only deletes the project's Competitors rows - does NOT touch question_pool, crawl_answers, gpower_scores, etc. Referencing data lingers; project_id becomes an orphan.
Same per-row delete loop in competitor replace (`for comp in old_result.scalars().all(): await db.delete(comp)`). Should be one DELETE WHERE project_id=... + bulk_insert_mappings.
Mixes fetch + delete + insert in a single transaction; small N is fine but blocks the connection.
After creating the project, loops `client_users_result.all()` and adds a ClientProjectPermissions per user individually (one INSERT per row). Should use bulk_insert_mappings or executemany.
f-string INTERVAL '{interval}' from a static map - safe, but raw SQL with the dynamic interval prevents plan caching.
`except Exception: main_rows = []` (bare except) on the brand_mention_daily query. The function then returns a successful response with empty series, masking DB outages.
Time-series chart endpoint, polled by client. Per-day data changes slowly; cache TTL = 60-300s is safe and dramatically reduces compute.

Loads ALL client_urls into memory, then extracts ALL crawl_answer.refer_info URLs via jsonb_array_elements with no LIMIT. For a busy project with 100k+ answers this is a full table scan with lateral expansion - very slow.
Two `except Exception:` blocks silently fall back to empty data. Operators get a coverage chart with 0 matched but no error - debugging is hard.
text(f"... INTERVAL '{interval}' ...") - safe but raw SQL; static map means we could pre-compute the SQL per range.
Three sequential queries (total, covered_count, covered_urls, uncovered_urls) for the same project. Could be folded into one with FILTER clauses.
Loads ALL covered/uncovered URLs into memory just to return them in the response (no pagination). With 10k+ URLs this is tens of MB serialized per call.
Coverage rate is a slow-changing aggregate; no cache despite the dashboard refreshing it frequently.
Separate count + paged select; could be one query with window function.
page_size=0 returns all rows for the project. For a project with thousands of published URLs this is unbounded memory.

Loops and `db.add(new_record)` per URL. Should use `bulk_insert_mappings` or Core `insert().values(list_of_dicts)` for 10x faster batch insert. Also re-parses urlparse twice (once in detect_platform, once for domain).
page_size=0 returns ALL questions with their crawl stats - unbounded. The crawl_stats GROUP BY already mitigates the per-row N+1, but the response payload itself becomes huge.
Question list is admin-heavy and changes slowly; no cache. Crawl stats can change frequently, so cache by (question_id, today) for 30-60s.
Per-question `db.add(question); await db.flush()` - one INSERT per row plus the flush round-trip. Use bulk_insert_mappings for batches >10.
Loads all existing question_content for the client (full table scan by client_id) to dedup. For a client with 10k+ questions this is unbounded and runs on every batch import.
9 sequential DELETE statements (analysis + crawler schemas) all inside one transaction. The crawl_answers and reference data can be millions of rows; this blocks the connection for minutes.
Could be merged into a single CTE-based DELETE with USING to delete in dependency order atomically.
Reads rpa (reference_paragraph_attribution) - the largest analysis table - with 3 LEFT JOINs and heavy aggregates on every admin call. No cache despite the time-range windowing.
f-string SQL construction; values are bound so safe, but the plan cache is invalidated per distinct where_clause string.
Count query and data query are separate round-trips; could be one query with a window function (`COUNT(*) OVER()`) to save a round-trip per page.
_get_reference_summary issues 2 separate aggregate queries (daily + attribution) per call. The fallback path adds another 1-2 queries. Hot admin endpoint with no cache.
Multiple f-string SQL with bound params; plan cache churn per distinct where_clause.
Domain stats query is `GROUP BY rsd.domain` over reference_source_daily - a large aggregate table. With wide time ranges and no LIMIT-by-domain this scans the whole window.
Fallback stats path also no cache; called when the primary path returns zero results, so first-time dashboards pay both costs.
Same dynamic SQL pattern.
F-string SQL with 14 FILTER columns generated dynamically from FEATURE_LABELS. Safe but breaks plan cache; should be a hand-written SQL with the 7 fixed features.
Feature analysis rarely changes between days; no cache. Could be a materialized view refreshed daily.

CRITICAL: Inside an `async def` function, creates a SYNC SQLAlchemy engine (`create_engine(_to_sync_db_url(db_url))`) and runs `db = SessionLocal(); ... db.commit()` - sync I/O in an async event loop. Each commit() blocks the loop. Must use AsyncSession or `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

On success, calls _watch_dcp_completion_and_sync_results which polls for up to 60 * 10s = 10 minutes, also with sync engine. Background task is fine for that, but combined with sync I/O it pegs a worker thread for 10 minutes.
Outer try/except is broad (`logger.exception(...)`) - swallows all errors. No monitoring/alerting on dcp_trigger_status='failed' besides an in-DB flag.
Polling loop uses SYNC engine (psycopg2) for 60 attempts * 10s. Blocks the async event loop each iteration. Should use the async engine and `await asyncio.sleep`.
Up to 10 minutes of polling per job, with sync DB calls. With concurrent jobs (concurrency limit 3) this can saturate the connection pool.
Each iteration re-runs sync_temp_crawl_results_from_answers_sync which iterates ALL answers and does per-row INSERT...ON CONFLICT. For 1000 answers = 1000 round-trips once completion detected.

Function name says `_sync` because it takes a sync Session, but it is invoked from the async `sync_temp_crawl_results_from_answers` in admin_temp_crawler_persistence. Two code paths (sync+async) for the same data sync - duplication and confusion.
Aggregation over crawl_answers + gpower_scores + brand_answer_metrics; no caching. Called from project detail page on every refresh.
page_size=0 returns ALL items (including full answer_text + answer_html). For a 10k-answer job, builds a 100MB+ Python list in one go, then serializes via the calling endpoint.
LATERAL joins on reference_source_daily and reference_sources per row - PostgreSQL handles this with Nested Loop, but for large result sets the per-row work dominates.
Result rows are immutable per job, no cache. Could be served from temp_crawl_results directly with a much simpler query.
Loops `items` (could be thousands) and for each item awaits `db.execute(text('INSERT ... ON CONFLICT'))` - one async round-trip per item. For 5000 answers = 5000 round-trips blocking the event loop.

Called from get_temp_crawl_detail, replay_temp_crawl_job, handle_temp_crawl_completion_callback, count_project_answers, build_project_answers_export. Repeatedly resyncs the same data on every read path.
Builds raw_response with `json.dumps(...)` in Python; PostgreSQL could build the jsonb with `jsonb_build_object(...)` in the same statement as the sync.

Loops every job_id in the project and calls sync_temp_crawl_results_from_answers (each one is a per-row INSERT loop). For a project with 10 jobs of 1000 answers each = 10000 round-trips on a single dashboard click.
Blocks the request handler. Should be a background task (the project export / count endpoints are user-facing).
Loads ALL formal + temp answer rows into memory (`rows.extend(await _query_formal_export_rows(...))`) and then writes to a BytesIO - unbounded export size, memory bomb on large projects.
Streams XLSX/CSV to BytesIO in-memory; for 50k rows the heap grows by hundreds of MB. Should stream to a file or response directly.
_query_formal_export_rows and _query_temp_export_rows have LATERAL joins over reference_source_daily/reference_sources per row - heavy on large exports.
Draft metadata is small but listed in list_temp_crawl_jobs which loads all jobs for the user on every poll. No cache for the list view.
For each user row, awaits _get_client_name + _get_client_projects (2 queries each). page_size=20 = 40 round-trips. Should be one JOIN with aggregation.
Hot admin endpoint, no cache. Client/Project name lookups are stable for seconds.
page_size=0 returns all users with all their projects - unbounded payload.
For each client_id in data.client_ids: create user, await db.flush(), then loop project_ids adding ClientProjectPermissions one at a time. With 3 clients * 5 projects = 15 awaits per request.
For each created user, then calls _get_client_name + _get_client_projects again to build the response. Could be one JOIN after the loop.
Loop `for pid in project_ids: db.add(ClientProjectPermissions(...))` - one INSERT per row. Use bulk_insert_mappings.
4 separate DELETE statements (OperatorPermissions, OperatorDataScope, UserLoginHistory, Users) in one transaction. With long login history tables the DELETE can be slow.

most_common_anti_patterns: N+1 queries inside per-row Python loops (14 files)
No caching on high-frequency admin dashboard endpoints (8 files)
Sync SQLAlchemy engine inside async functions (2 files)
Silent Exception swallow masking DB outages (2 files)
